newsitem.title: UK: Alliance rules out overseas acquisition.
newsitem.headline: Alliance rules out overseas acquisition.

text.p: Alliance & Leicester, the British building society-turned bank, on Friday confirmed it was still looking at the possibility of acquisitions but ruled out a purchase overseas.
"No-one here is taking any foreign language courses," finance director Richard Pym told Reuters.
Returning cash to shareholders remained an option, admitted Pym, but he refused to be drawn into committing the group to a timetable.
"We want to grow the business. That can be by acquisition or organically. We've shown in the first half that there is organic growth capacity in this business," he said.
Pym was speaking after A&L marked its first set of results as a publicly listed company with a three percent fall in first-half, pre-tax profits to 178 million pounds, ahead of analyst forecasts.
"If we don't use capital for acquisitions or organic growth, we will consider returning it to shareholders but it's too early to be talking about share buybacks," said Pym.

"We have a lot of thinking and a lot of planning to do before we get to that stage. We are committed to liberating the value of this business. Clearly there is great capacity in this organisation to trade on lower capital ratios."
Management had a job to manage the business for the maximum value over the long term, he said, refusing to set the group "artificial" deadlines.
A&L had a hurdle rate based on its weighted average cost of capital which would determine the price it was willing to pay, he said.
But an overseas acquisition is out.
"We have no wish to invest our shareholders money overseas - if they want to buy an overseas bank they can buy shares in that - they don't need A&L to buy the shares on their behalf."

At its interim results last week the Woolwich described the possibility of UK acquisitions as problematic and said it may "cherry-pick" in France where it already had a foothold and where valuations are lower.
A&L's acquisition strategy was based on acquiring either more customers or more products to sell to existing customers, said Pym.
"It's a very simple strategy and it's one we're going to hold to."
A&L has seen some outflow of business since its conversion in April but in the last few weeks windfall withdrawals have fallen significantly.
Overall, customer accounts were almost identical to year-end -- less than 100 million pounds lower at 18.1 billion pounds.
Net mortgage lending increased sharply from last year to 527 million pounds and Pym said the group would not sacrifice return on capital for market share.
"We have a very simple pricing criteria. We have profit requirements and when we can add mortgages we will, at that price."
Staff reductions will continue in the second half though not at the rate in the first six months.

"We will reduce staff levels in a number of areas but we're also building staff in insurance and leasing. Overall staff numbers will be somewhat down on where they are now but the big shift seen in first half won't be repeated in the second half," said Pym.
A&L recently launched in its own general insurance business which will be a core part of the product portfolio going forward.
The group will selectively take some underwriting positions to test the market and, with a collection mechanism for the premiums, it believes it has competitive advantages.
Girobank produced level profit for the first half and the strategy remains to develop business within Girobank, selling specialist banking products to its existing customer base.
Last November it bought Sovereign Finance - a leasing business and A&L intends to leverage that by selling leases into existing Girobank commercial customers.
-- Simon Cowell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7721
